a: Multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalisation (pre-LN in most modern LLMs). Attention mixes information across tokens; the FFN transforms each token's vector.

q: How do Transformers know word order?
a: Through positional information: sinusoidal or learned position vectors added to embeddings (original Transformer, BERT, GPT-2), or rotary position embeddings (RoPE) that rotate queries and keys so attention depends on relative distance (LLaMA, Mistral), or ALiBi biases.

During generation, keys and values of past tokens don't change, so each layer stores them and only computes q, k, v for the new token. It turns per-token cost from re-processing the whole prefix into one step, but uses memory: about 0.5 MB per token for LLaMA-2-7B in FP16.

q: Why is LLM decoding memory-bound rather than compute-bound?
a: Each new token needs only a little computation but must read all model weights and the KV cache from GPU memory. Memory bandwidth, not FLOPs, limits speed. Batching many requests, quantisation and GQA help.

Post-LN normalises after adding the residual (original Transformer) and is harder to train deep without warmup. Pre-LN normalises the sub-layer input and keeps a clean residual path, which is more stable; most modern LLMs use pre-norm (often RMSNorm).

q: Where are most of a Transformer's parameters?
a: In the feed-forward networks: with a 4× expansion they have about 8d² parameters per block vs 4d² for attention, so roughly two-thirds of the non-embedding parameters.

q: Why did decoder-only models become the default for LLMs?
a: One simple objective (next-token prediction) that uses all text and scales smoothly, natural generation, strong in-context learning, and the ability to handle classification or extraction by generating the answer. KV caching also makes generation efficient.
